oneSentence: An authorised task or scope of work formally given to a person, group or organisation by a competent authority.
plainExplanation:
A mandate tells someone what they have been authorised to do. It usually comes from a formal authority, such as a court, parliament, board or United Nations organ. In UN settings, it often comes from an adopted text such as a resolution or decision.

What goes in is an instruction from an authority. That instruction normally names the actor, the task, the subject area, and sometimes the time period, reporting duties or limits. For example, a text might ask the Secretariat to prepare a report on AI governance options before a certain meeting.

What happens next is that the person or body checks the exact wording and acts within that authorised scope. The wording matters. A broad phrase such as “explore options” gives more room than a narrow phrase such as “draft recommendations on three topics”.

What comes out is authorised action that can be traced back to an adopted authority. This is why people ask, “What is the mandate?” They are checking whether a meeting, report, negotiation or project is actually authorised, and how far that authority reaches.

A mandate is often confused with terms of reference. Terms of reference usually describe how a group will work in more operational detail. A mandate gives authority for the work. Terms of reference usually describe the job and how a group, project or process will operate.

everydayAnalogy.title: A school fair organising letter
everydayAnalogy.story: A school principal gives a student committee a signed letter saying they may organise the school fair, use the assembly hall on Friday, and spend up to 500 units from the activities budget. The committee can book tables and invite clubs because the letter authorises those actions. But it cannot repaint the hall or collect extra fees from families, because the letter does not authorise that. When questions come up, everyone goes back to the exact wording of the letter.

everydayAnalogy.limitation: A school letter usually comes from one clear authority and applies inside one institution. UN mandates can be negotiated by many Member States, written in carefully balanced language, and shaped by political context. They may also involve reporting lines, budget implications and legal questions that a simple school example does not capture.

visual.title: How a mandate turns agreed words into authorised action
visual.learningObjective: Show how a formal instruction from an authority creates a defined scope for action and a basis for checking whether a task is authorised.
visual.description: A four-step horizontal diagram. Read left to right: an authority adopts a text, the text assigns a task, the receiving actor interprets the wording, and action happens within set limits. Each step shows both what is added and what is constrained.

steps.label: 1. Authority speaks
steps.explanation: A recognised body adopts a formal instruction, often in an agreed document.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a document icon under a group-of-people icon labelled 'authority'. Add a short tag: 'approved text'.

steps.label: 2. Task is assigned
steps.explanation: The text names who should act and what they are authorised to do.
steps.visualInstruction: Show an arrow to a second panel with a person or office icon and three small labels: 'who', 'what', 'by when'.

steps.label: 3. Wording sets limits
steps.explanation: The exact language defines scope. Some actions are included; others are outside the mandate.
steps.visualInstruction: Split the panel into two columns labelled 'inside scope' and 'outside scope'. Use ticks and crosses next to simple action icons.

steps.label: 4. Action and accountability
steps.explanation: The actor carries out work that can be traced back to the authorising text and may report back.
steps.visualInstruction: Show a report icon returning by arrow to the authority, with a caption: 'action linked to authority'.

visual.interaction: Hover or tap each step to reveal example phrases such as 'prepare a report', 'convene consultations' and 'outside current mandate'.
visual.accessibilityDescription: This diagram explains mandate as a sequence of four linked stages. First, a recognised authority adopts a formal text. Second, that text assigns a task to a person, office or group, often stating who acts, what they should do and sometimes by when. Third, the exact wording defines the limits of authority, so some actions are inside scope and others are not. Fourth, the receiving actor carries out work and may report back, so the action can be traced to the original authorisation.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: A static four-panel diagram shown left to right with arrows between panels. Panel 1 shows an authority and approved text. Panel 2 shows the named actor and task. Panel 3 shows actions inside and outside scope. Panel 4 shows action and reporting back.

workedExample.scenario: An evaluation office receives a governing-board decision requesting an assessment of an AI-assisted translation pilot and recommendations for any future use.
workedExample.input: Adopted decision: the evaluation office is requested to assess the completed pilot, consult participating offices and submit findings and recommendations at the board's next session.
process: The adopted decision supplies the authority and identifies the evaluation office as the responsible actor.
The authorised task is assessment. It includes consulting participating offices and preparing findings and recommendations.
The scope is the completed pilot, and the deadline is the board's next session.
The office may request records needed for the assessment, subject to applicable access and confidentiality rules. It may not extend the pilot or procure a replacement system under this mandate.
workedExample.result: The evaluation report is within mandate. Renewing licences, expanding the pilot or directing offices to adopt the tool is not. Those actions would need authority from the competent decision-maker and the relevant operational approvals.

unWorkplaceExample.scenario: At the annual workplan review, a desk officer in a regional bureau checks a proposed activity to develop an AI tool for analysing programme reports. The workplan cites a governing-body decision that requested options and recommendations, but did not authorise development or deployment.
unWorkplaceExample.relevance: The desk officer traces the proposed activity back to the adopted text and flags the gap for the chief of section. The bureau may research options and prepare recommendations, but building a tool would require separate authority, resources and approvals. A workplan can organise delivery of a mandate. It cannot quietly enlarge one.
unWorkplaceExample.caution: Mandate is not the same as technical feasibility or managerial enthusiasm. Before work begins, confirm the authorising text, responsible actor, specified function and applicable limits. Separate approvals may still be required for budget, procurement, data protection and information security.

whyItMatters:
A mandate is one of the quickest ways to tell whether a piece of work has proper authority behind it. If you understand the mandate, you can judge what a team may do now, what needs new approval, and where responsibility sits.

This matters in meetings, project design and negotiations. A broad mandate can allow exploration and coordination. A narrow mandate can prevent overreach but may slow action if new approval is needed.

For non-specialists, the practical question is simple: is this activity authorised, by whom, and within what limits? In AI governance, that question affects whether a body can study an issue, draft guidance, convene experts, support capacity-building or recommend rules.
whereYouMayHearIt: During informals on draft General Assembly text
At an annual workplan review in a regional bureau
In a front-office clearance meeting on a briefing note
When an ICT governance board reviews the scope of a proposed pilot

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A mandate means someone must do whatever seems useful on the topic.
commonMisconceptions.correction: No. It authorises action only within the scope set by the formal text. If the wording says 'study options', that does not automatically authorise implementation, funding commitments or new negotiations.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A mandate and terms of reference are the same thing.
commonMisconceptions.correction: They are related but different. A mandate is the formal authority and broad scope. Terms of reference usually set out practical details such as membership, methods, timeline or deliverables.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: If an issue is important, a UN office automatically has a mandate to act on it.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Importance alone does not create authority. In the UN, offices and bodies usually need a mandate from the relevant organ or governing body before taking specific formal action.

simpleVsTechnical.simple: A mandate is formal permission plus instructions about what someone is allowed and expected to do.
simpleVsTechnical.technical: In governance and institutional settings, a mandate is the legally or procedurally recognised authorisation conferred by a competent body on a person, office, subsidiary body or organisation to perform specified functions within defined substantive, temporal and sometimes geographic limits. It is normally expressed in an adopted instrument such as a resolution, decision, charter provision or governing-board text. Operationally, a mandate answers at least four questions: who is authorised, to do what, on which subject, and under what constraints or reporting obligations. The scope may be broad or narrow depending on the verbs used, for example 'consider', 'monitor', 'prepare a report', 'facilitate dialogue' or 'develop recommendations'. A mandate does not by itself settle every procedural detail, budget line or work method; those may be addressed separately. In UN practice, questions about whether an activity is 'within mandate' affect legitimacy, resource use, accountability and whether further intergovernmental approval is needed.

keyTakeaway: A mandate is the recognised authority to act. Its wording determines who may do what, for what purpose, within which limits. A workplan or managerial request cannot silently expand it.

quickCheck.question: Which statement best describes a mandate?
options: A detailed meeting schedule for a working group
Formal authority that assigns a task and sets its scope
An informal suggestion from experts about what would be useful
A public announcement that a topic is politically important
quickCheck.explanation: A mandate is about authorised scope. It comes from a recognised authority and tells an actor what they may or should do. Schedules, expert suggestions and public announcements may matter, but they do not by themselves create that authority.

issues.problem: The definition restricts the source of a mandate to a recognised or competent body. An authorised office-holder or other competent authority can also confer a mandate. The school-principal analogy itself uses an individual authority.
issues.fix: Replace “recognised body” and “competent body” with “competent authority”.

issues.problem: Calling a resolution or decision an “agreed text” is inaccurate. A text may be adopted through a vote despite objections, so adoption does not necessarily indicate agreement or consensus. This wording also blurs the stated distinction from consensus.
issues.fix: Use “adopted text” in the explanation. In the visual, use: “A recognised body issues a formal instruction, often through an adopted document.”

issues.problem: The claim that a mandate produces “legitimate action” overstates what a mandate establishes. Action may be authorised by a mandate yet still breach other legal, procedural or budgetary requirements.

The page twice characterises a mandate as higher-level or broad in contrast with terms of reference. Mandates can be narrow, as the page itself later states. The actual distinction is authority versus the document that sets the job, scope, roles, timeline and outputs.
issues.fix: In the explanation, use: “A mandate gives authority for the work. Terms of reference usually describe the job and how a group, project or process will operate.” In the correction, use: “They are related but different. A mandate gives authority for the work. Terms of reference set its job, scope, roles, timeline and expected outputs.”

issues.problem: The distractors are implausible and do not test the distinctions the page claims to teach. Only one option mentions formal authority, an assigned task or scope, so the answer is obvious without understanding mandate, resolution, consensus or terms of reference.
issues.fix: Replace the options with: [“A text adopted to record a shared position”, “Formal authority that assigns a task and sets its scope”, “A document setting a group’s roles, methods and outputs”, “Adoption when no delegation present formally objects”]. Keep correctOptionIndex as 1.
